validate

/VAL-ih-dayt/ - the stress falls on VAL · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Validate means to confirm that something is accurate, sound, or officially acceptable — to put it through a check it must pass.

Crash tests validated the redesigned bumper months before the first car left the line.

Example

When the marathon winner beat the state record by forty seconds, nobody doubted the clock — they doubted the course. Officials spent the next week validating it: re-riding the route with calibrated measuring wheels and checking every turn against the certified map, and only when the course itself had passed inspection did the record stand.

Validate fits because what gets confirmed is soundness against a standard: the course must measure what a marathon must measure, and the checking is the whole point. Corroborate would need a second witness telling the same story; authenticate, taught earlier in this unit, would ask whether the course was genuine rather than whether it held up. Validation is the passed test.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

confirm: To confirm is to establish that something is true — a fact, a booking, a rumor. Validate is narrower and more procedural: you confirm a fact, but you validate a thing against a test or a standard — a method, a ticket, a result.

endorse: To endorse is to declare public support — a vote of confidence from a person. Validation is a demonstration, not a vote: the thing itself passes a check, whoever happens to be cheering for it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

debunk: to show that a claim or method is false

refute: to prove an argument or claim wrong

Where it sits · how official the confirmation is

support → validate → certify

support vs. validate: Support is weaker than validate: evidence that supports a method just leans its way, while validating the method means it has actually passed the checks that could have sunk it.

certify vs. validate: Certify goes further than validate — a validated result has passed its test, but a certified one carries an authority's official seal, with the confirmation itself written into a document.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — valid: strong, sound (Latin validus, from valere, 'to be strong, to be well')

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do

Put it together: Valid (strong, sound — Latin validus) + -ate = to make or declare strong. Roman law asked whether an act was validus, strong enough to stand; to validate something is to test that strength and, finding it, let the thing stand — a result, a ticket, a license now officially able to bear weight.

Use the root in a new word: valor: The citation for valor ran just two sentences, and the old medic kept it in a drawer.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Validate is the workhorse of labs, registrars, and parking garages: something is checked against a standard and passes — data, tickets, credentials, results. Two cautions. Don't reach for it when you mean corroborate, this unit's second-source verb: validation needs a test, not another witness. And its softer modern use — validating someone's feelings — is real English, but in analytical writing keep the word for checks that something could fail.
